title: Thoughts on Word Problems + Pictures
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane records his takeaways from a Global Math Department talk by Nicora Placa on using diagrams to make sense of word problems, adding his own thinking. His main claim is that drawing a picture is a concrete, specific tool that supports hard problem solving, whereas telling students to persevere or try another method is disheartening when they have no method to try. He ties this to working memory, since diagrams reduce what students must hold in their heads and so improve accuracy and access to more complex questions. He also argues that grit is taught by giving students specific tools they can use to be gritty, not by exhorting them. Finally he suggests pictures can introduce algebraic thinking early, using a bicycle-savings problem to show the difference between subtract-then-divide and reasoning about unknowns. It is a brief teacher-practitioner post, and the notes are partly his own extensions of the talk.
points: Diagrams reduce working memory load, which Kane links to higher accuracy, access to more complex questions and better learning.
Vague advice like persevere or try a different method teaches struggling students that they cannot do hard maths, while draw a picture is a concrete next step.
Kane says grit is built by handing students specific tools rather than telling them grit matters.
Separating the workspace with a line is one habit he has seen strong students use to organise their thinking on complex word problems.
Pictures can introduce algebraic reasoning as early as fifth grade, easing later algebra, as in the bicycle savings problem.
quotes: Diagrams reduce what students hold in their head. In more technical jargon, it reduces the working memory load. Increases accuracy, the complexity of questions students can access, and quality of learning.

One of the best things some of my students do in complicated word problems is to draw a line to separate their workspace. It's neat, it's logical, and it keeps work organized in a way that reflects the thinking they are doing

But telling kids to think about something, to persevere when they're hopelessly confused, to try a different method when they never had a method to begin with, is enormously disheartening. It teaches, with a very rapid feedback loop, that they are incapable of doing hard math, and so there's no point in trying.
Draw a picture is concrete and specific. It's not "try a different method", it's "if you get stuck on a word problem, try drawing a picture".

I don't think I can do that by telling kids that grit is important, or telling them that if they just have enough grit they will be successful. I think part of teaching grit is giving kids specific tools that they can use to be gritty.

Pictures can be a great way to introduce very basic algebraic thinking very early on. This is a big step on the staircase of abstraction, and the earlier kids are exposed to algebraic ways of solving problems, the more skills they will have in algebraic representation when they really need them in the upper grades.
